definition: A named vocabulary of whole-spine curvature shapes — described by the letter they resemble (a C-shape, an S-shape breakdown, a reverse-C-shape) — used across the extreme-breakdown-extreme structure of one shape-changing beat: a slight C-shape building before impact, a full C-shape at the impact extreme, an S-shape breakdown in the recovery, and a reverse-C-shape at the recovery extreme.
purpose: Give the whole spine a visible, contrasting shape at each phase of an impact-and-recovery beat, so the body reads as flexible and physically affected rather than a rigid rod that merely relocates.
visible_effect: The torso's silhouette curves noticeably to one side (C), reverses through a mild S-curve, then curves the other way (reverse-C), rather than staying straight while only the limbs and overall position change.
psychological_or_gameplay_effect: Without any spine curvature at all, a character "feels robotically stiff" even if the limbs and timing are otherwise correct — the shape change is what sells that the body itself absorbed and is recovering from the impact.
physical_interpretation: An approximation of how a flexible spine actually bends under an off-center impact and then rebounds — contrasting extreme shapes make the before/after states of that bend legible even at a glance.
use_cases: any impact-and-recovery beat (a landing, a hit reaction, a fall) where contrasting body shapes at the extremes would sell the physical effect
a breakdown between two contrasting extreme shapes, where an S-curve intermediate shape helps carry the weight of the transition
non_use_cases: a mechanical or rigid-spine character where the torso should not curve at all
a subtle, low-key beat where a strong C/S/reverse-C contrast would read as overacted
interactions: Squash & stretch — the video pairs this same beat with squash (compressing down into the C-shape at impact) and stretch (extending back out of the reverse-C on recovery); the two techniques are applied to the SAME beat but are structurally different: squash/stretch is a volume/scale effect Cadence cannot represent directly, while a spine curve is pure joint rotation Cadence already fully supports
Structural understanding — spine shape is a direct, visible expression of that card's balance/volume concern, specific to the torso chain
Exaggeration — the two contrasting extreme shapes (C, then reverse-C) are themselves a selective-amplification choice: the spine is exaggerated at the extremes and settles between them

style_variations.realistic: curvature kept subtle — a slight, physically plausible bend rather than a graphic C/S shape
style_variations.cartoon: the letter-shapes can be pushed further and held longer, closer to the source example

cadence_representation: A genuinely strong fit, unlike squash & stretch's own mesh-deformation problem: a whole-spine curve is nothing more than a coordinated sequence of ordinary joint rotations down the spine chain (however many spine joints the rig provides), which Cadence's rigid Motor6D rig already represents natively — no mesh deformation is needed at all, unlike the compression/extension half of the same beat. Nothing currently names "C-shape / S-shape / reverse-C-shape" as a posing vocabulary a caller could request, but every rotation needed to build one is already an ordinary keyframe.
control_surface: Direct per-joint rotation down a spine chain via `set_keyframe`/`authorMotion`'s pose-per-phase mechanism; no named "spine curve shape" vocabulary term exists to request one declaratively.
detection_and_measurement_methods: None dedicated — `ai/pose.js`'s line-of-action measurement is the closest existing concept (a single sweeping curve summarizing a pose's dominant visual line) but nothing specifically measures spine-chain curvature as its own quantity or classifies it against a named letter-shape.
generation_or_modification_methods: None declaratively — a spine curve can already be hand-authored as a sequence of joint rotations through `authorMotion`, but no strategy derives a C/S/reverse-C shape from a higher-level request.
failure_modes: keeping the spine straight through an impact-and-recovery beat, producing the "robotically stiff" read this video names directly
using the same shape at both extremes (no contrast between the impact and recovery shapes), losing the visual legibility the contrast is meant to provide
roblox_considerations: Directly exportable: any Roblox rig with more than one spine/torso joint (R15's `LowerTorso`/`UpperTorso` split, or a custom multi-bone spine) can carry a real spine curve; an R6/single-torso rig has no chain to curve at all, which is worth naming as a real rig-dependent limitation distinct from anything about Cadence itself.
examples: Miguel's spine curling into a C-shape as he slides into Hector's hip, flipping into a reverse-C-shape on landing, with an S-shape breakdown between them (video @ 4:59–5:34, a C-shaped landing pose directly confirmed on screen at t=5:06)
the same beat's squash (compressing down at the C-shape impact) and stretch (extending back out of the reverse-C on recovery) layered on top of the spine-curve shapes themselves (video @ 5:48–6:12)
evidence_status: video: https://youtu.be/fFf8EsPC_ws @ 4:59–5:34 — Rusty Animator names the C-shape, S-shape breakdown, and reverse-C-shape explicitly while stepping through the Pixar *Coco* clip; a frame at t=5:06 in this session's sample directly confirms a visible C-shaped spine curve on Miguel mid-landing; experimental until validated
